summary: North Brother Island Light, a wooden tower lit in 1869 in the East River; discontinued 1953; island closed to the public under NYC Parks; General Slocum fire nearby, 1904.

light.characteristic: fixed white (1869); five seconds light, five seconds eclipse (from 15 May 1894)

lens.note: Fourth order from 1899 (replacing a fifth-order lens). The 1869 optic is disputed: archive gives fourth-order Fresnel; LighthouseFriends gives sixth-order.

structures.status: upper tower and lantern room removed 1953; dwelling collapsed
structures.note: Light moved onto the metal fog-bell tower in 1953 (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Not open to the public; island overseen by the New York City Parks Department and designated conservation land (bird sanctuary).

facts.ownership: New York City Parks Department oversees the island (Vanity Fair, citing Payne).

events.note: Congress approves $5,000 for a light on the Brothers; the owner would not sell; funds returned after the state did not act.
Appropriations of $8,500 (1866) and $7,500 (1867) for the station.
Title to the southern tip of the island acquired.
Two-story keeper's dwelling with mansard roof and integral octagonal wooden tower.
Light first shown November 1869 (LighthouseFriends); archive gives 1869 as the year the original lens was installed.
Fence built to separate the lighthouse from Riverside Hospital.
Board's report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1892 recommends a beacon near the island's north end, which would need no expense for a site.
From fixed white to five seconds of light and five seconds of eclipse (15 May 1894). New lens with occulting clock installed.
New lens with occulting clock; new bell tower and Gamewell fog-bell apparatus.
Fourth-order lens substituted for the fifth-order lens; intensity increased (29 November 1899).
Brick oil house built; various repairs.
Keeper Joseph D. Meade leaves the island on 5 January 1903 and is never found; authorities suspect foul play (LighthouseFriends).

Excursion steamer General Slocum burns near North Brother Island on 15 June 1904; run aground in a small cove on the far side of the island; over 1,000 dead (LighthouseFriends); early Tribune headline gave possibly 700.
Light mounted on the metal fog-bell tower; lantern room and top portion of the tower removed; replaced by a skeletal light (archive disposition).
Island's last institutional use, a juvenile drug-treatment center, closes; the island is then abandoned (Vanity Fair, citing Payne).

notes_for_editor: 1) Status: the record's conflict list says OpenStreetMap maps a standing structure; LighthouseFriends says the lighthouse collapsed; the archive says the tower was removed from the dwelling in 1953 and the dwelling collapsed. I did not read the OSM way or any recent aerial image; the story says only what the archive and LighthouseFriends record. 2) Original optic: the archive gives fourth-order Fresnel in 1869; LighthouseFriends gives sixth-order fixed white; the Board's 1900 report shows a fifth-order lens in use until 29 Nov 1899 (fourth-order substituted). The 1869 optic is unresolved. 3) Pre-1891 history (1829 appropriation, 1848 and 1866-68 steps, 1869 first light, 1883 fence, 1889 fog bell) rests on LighthouseFriends alone: the corpus Light-House Board volumes start in 1891. 4) Meade (1902-03): LighthouseFriends only. A Chronicling America search of NY papers for 1903 with 'Meade' and 'North Brother' returned no hits; the story attributes the account to LighthouseFriends. 5) General Slocum: the Tribune says the fire began as the boat passed Sunken Meadows (about 10 a.m.); LighthouseFriends places it at Hell Gate. Both are given. The final death toll is not confirmed in any primary source I read; LighthouseFriends says more than 1,000. The Tribune's early headline says possibly 700. Consider a later Tribune issue for the final count. 6) Captain's account of the island landing is from LighthouseFriends; the Tribune OCR is garbled on that point. 7) Privacy: LighthouseFriends's 1935 anecdote about a keeper's daughter and a man rescued from the water is omitted (private people, no station role). Typhoid Mary is named only as Vanity Fair names her (historical figure, died 1938, not a keeper). Coast Guard roster names are published archive names with no personal detail. 8) The Vanity Fair piece is a June 2015 reprint of an Atlas Obscura interview with Christopher Payne; the footnote gives the Vanity Fair address. 9) Copyrighted: LighthouseFriends and Vanity Fair paraphrased; no quotation runs longer than a short phrase. 10) The Life-Saving Service's North Brother entries (wreck tables) were not used. 11) Fact-check 2026-10-27: the Board's beacon proposal (scan p.406) sits in the report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1892, not 1891; the volume's 1892 report title page precedes it, so the story and the 1891 event now say 1892. 12) range_nm 4 removed: no cited source gives a range. 13) Roster lines for Donnelly, Joyce, Anderson, Foley, Freeman and Miner were added to the evidence (they match the archive roster exactly); the story names Donnelly and Joyce but not the USCG names. 14) The landing: LighthouseFriends puts the grounding in a small cove on the far side of the island (the wreck event earlier said north shore). 15) The Tribune's headline and its unofficial 'more than seven hundred' estimate are both cited; LighthouseFriends' 'over 1,000' is cited separately and the story does not reconcile them.
